blocks.content: Singleton looks like the easiest pattern in the entire catalog. One class, one static instance, one method to fetch it.
Then you add a second thread and the whole thing quietly falls apart. Two threads can both check the instance, both see nothing there, and both go ahead and build their own copy.

Now you have two loggers, two config objects, or two connection pools that were supposed to be exactly one. The bug does not show up on your laptop. It shows up in production, under load, at the worst possible time.
This lesson walks through why the classic lazy Singleton breaks under concurrency, the fixes that actually work, the ones that only look like they work, and which approach to reach for by default.

A race condition in Singleton creation happens when two threads both read the instance field as null before either one has finished writing to it, so both threads create and both believe they hold the only copy.
Nothing here needs exotic hardware or a huge cluster to reproduce. A single machine with more than one CPU core, running ordinary application code under real traffic, is enough.
That is what makes this such a common interview question and such a common production incident. The fix is small, but skipping it is easy to miss in review.
1. The Race Condition In Lazy Initialization
blocks.text: 1. The Race Condition In Lazy Initialization

blocks.content: The classic lazy Singleton delays creating the object until someone actually asks for it. That is fine in a single threaded program.
The moment two threads can call getInstance at the same time, the check and the create step stop being one atomic operation.

Lazy initialization exists for a good reason, to avoid paying for an object nobody ends up needing. The problem is not laziness itself, it is doing the check and the create without any coordination between threads.
Step by step, how it breaks
blocks.text: Step by step, how it breaks

blocks.content: ["Thread A calls getInstance and reads instance as null.","Before Thread A finishes building the object, the scheduler switches to Thread B.","Thread B calls getInstance and also reads instance as null, because Thread A has not written anything yet.","Both threads now proceed to build a new object.","Whichever thread writes last wins the field, but both objects were fully constructed, and any work the first object did before being overwritten is silently lost."]
items: Thread A calls getInstance and reads instance as null.
Before Thread A finishes building the object, the scheduler switches to Thread B.
Thread B calls getInstance and also reads instance as null, because Thread A has not written anything yet.
Both threads now proceed to build a new object.
Whichever thread writes last wins the field, but both objects were fully constructed, and any work the first object did before being overwritten is silently lost.

codes.python:
import threading

class Logger:
    _instance = None

    def __init__(self):
        pass  # pretend this opens a file handle

    @classmethod
    def get_instance(cls):
        if cls._instance is None:      # both threads can pass this check
            cls._instance = Logger()   # both threads can reach this line
        return cls._instance

# Two threads calling Logger.get_instance() at nearly the same
# time can both see _instance as None before either assignment
# happens, due to the GIL switching between bytecode instructions
# at exactly the wrong moment. The result is the same as Java:
# two separate Logger objects, one of them silently discarded.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    results = [None] * 8
    threads = []

    def worker(idx):
        results[idx] = Logger.get_instance()

    for i in range(8):
        t = threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(i,))
        threads.append(t)

    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()

    distinct_instances = len(set(id(r) for r in results))
    print(f"Distinct Logger instances created: {distinct_instances}")
    print("(Under real concurrent load this can be more than 1, "
          "which is the whole point of this example.)")

blocks.title: Why this is worse than a normal bug
blocks.content: The two objects usually behave identically for a while, so the code passes every test that runs on one thread. The failure only appears under real concurrent load, which is exactly when nobody wants to be debugging it.
What actually breaks downstream

["A connection pool Singleton created twice means two separate pools quietly splitting your traffic, each with its own connection limit.","A cache Singleton created twice means writes to one copy are invisible to reads from the other copy, producing stale or inconsistent data.","A configuration Singleton created twice can mean half your application reads settings loaded before a config reload, and half reads settings loaded after."]
items: A connection pool Singleton created twice means two separate pools quietly splitting your traffic, each with its own connection limit.
A cache Singleton created twice means writes to one copy are invisible to reads from the other copy, producing stale or inconsistent data.
A configuration Singleton created twice can mean half your application reads settings loaded before a config reload, and half reads settings loaded after.

blocks.content: 2. The Naive Fix, Synchronizing The Whole Method
blocks.text: 2. The Naive Fix, Synchronizing The Whole Method

blocks.content: The instinctive fix is to slap a lock around the entire method. In Java that means marking getInstance as synchronized.
This does solve the race condition completely. Only one thread can be inside the method at any moment, so the null check and the object creation become effectively atomic.
Why it actually works

["Every call to getInstance must first acquire the same lock.","Only one thread can hold that lock at a time, all other callers wait.","By the time a waiting thread gets the lock, the first thread has already finished creating the instance, so the null check now correctly returns false for everyone after the first call."]
items: Every call to getInstance must first acquire the same lock.
Only one thread can hold that lock at a time, all other callers wait.
By the time a waiting thread gets the lock, the first thread has already finished creating the instance, so the null check now correctly returns false for everyone after the first call.

blocks.content: Why it is still the wrong fix
blocks.text: Why it is still the wrong fix

blocks.content: The instance only needs protecting during the one time it gets created. After that first call, every future call is just reading a field that never changes again.

A synchronized method forces every single call, forever, to acquire and release a lock, even the millionth call happening long after the object was built. Under heavy concurrent traffic that lock becomes a bottleneck that serializes work that did not need to be serialized.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499322368-673396176.png
blocks.alt: Three separate calls to getInstance all queueing on the same shared lock, one at a time, even long after the instance already exists

blocks.title: The cost in numbers
blocks.text: Picture a getInstance call that happens ten million times a second across a busy service. With a synchronized method, every one of those ten million calls competes for the same lock, even though the object was created on call number one and never changes again. That is ten million unnecessary lock acquisitions for a field that is effectively read only after startup.

blocks.content: A tempting but wrong shortcut
Some developers try to reduce the cost by only synchronizing the null check, not the whole method, hoping to shrink the critical section.

That does not work. If the check and the creation are not protected by the same lock together, the two threads can still both pass the check before either one finishes creating the object, and the original race condition comes right back.
3. Double Checked Locking
Double checked locking keeps the lock, but shrinks what it protects and adds a second check so the lock is only ever paid for once.
The name comes from checking the null condition twice, once before locking and once after.
The two checks and why each one exists
blocks.text: The two checks and why each one exists

blocks.content: ["First check, outside the lock. If the instance already exists, which is true for the overwhelming majority of calls, return it immediately without ever touching the lock.","Lock only happens if the first check found instance still null, meaning we might be in the middle of creating it.","Second check, inside the lock. Another thread may have already created the instance while we were waiting for the lock, so we check again before creating a second time.","Only if the second check also finds null do we actually build the object."]
items: First check, outside the lock. If the instance already exists, which is true for the overwhelming majority of calls, return it immediately without ever touching the lock.
Lock only happens if the first check found instance still null, meaning we might be in the middle of creating it.
Second check, inside the lock. Another thread may have already created the instance while we were waiting for the lock, so we check again before creating a second time.
Only if the second check also finds null do we actually build the object.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783494602222-608939424.png
blocks.alt: Two threads racing to check and create a Singleton instance at the same time, resulting in two separate objects

blocks.content: Why the lock name matters

The synchronized block locks on Logger.class, a single object shared by every thread in the JVM for that class. If two different pieces of code locked on two different objects, the lock would provide no real protection at all, since the threads would never actually contend with each other.
4. Why Volatile Is Not Optional Here
blocks.text: 4. Why Volatile Is Not Optional Here

blocks.content: Double checked locking has a famous history of being subtly broken, and the missing piece was always the volatile keyword.
Without volatile, the compiler and the processor are allowed to reorder the steps inside new Logger for performance reasons, as long as the reordering looks harmless to a single thread.
The reordering problem in detail
Creating an object is really three separate steps under the hood.
["Allocate memory for the new object.","Run the constructor to initialize its fields.","Point the instance variable at that memory."]
items: Allocate memory for the new object.
Run the constructor to initialize its fields.
Point the instance variable at that memory.

blocks.content: A compiler is free to reorder steps two and three, because from the point of view of the thread doing the creating, the end result looks identical either way.

The danger is a second thread reading instance in between. If step three has happened but step two has not, that second thread sees instance as non null and returns it immediately, skipping the lock entirely, even though the object it just received is only partially constructed.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499324563-35900188.png
blocks.alt: Allocating memory and publishing the reference before the constructor finishes, letting a second thread read a half constructed object

blocks.title: What volatile actually guarantees
blocks.content: Marking the field volatile stops the compiler and processor from reordering the write to that field relative to the writes that happened before it. It also guarantees that once one thread writes to a volatile field, every other thread that later reads it sees that write, along with everything that happened before it. Together those two guarantees are exactly what double checked locking needs to be safe.
The historical name for this bug
blocks.text: The historical name for this bug

blocks.content: This exact failure mode is documented widely enough to have its own name, the double checked locking problem, discussed at length in early 2000s Java literature before the memory model was fixed in Java 5.

Before Java 5, volatile did not even provide the guarantees described above, which meant double checked locking was broken in Java no matter what you did. That history is why some older codebases still avoid the pattern entirely.
5. Eager Initialization
The simplest fix for the whole problem is to stop being lazy about it.
Create the instance the moment the class is loaded, before any thread could possibly race to create it. The class loader handles the one-time-only guarantee for you.
There is a real cost too, since the object gets built even if nothing ever calls getInstance during that run.
This is often the very first fix engineers reach for once they understand why the lazy version is broken.
Why this sidesteps the race entirely
blocks.text: Why this sidesteps the race entirely

blocks.content: ["The class loading mechanism itself guarantees that a class is initialized exactly once, even under concurrent access from multiple threads.","By the time any thread calls getInstance, the instance field is already set, there is no null window to race inside.","No lock, no volatile, no double checking, needed anywhere."]
items: The class loading mechanism itself guarantees that a class is initialized exactly once, even under concurrent access from multiple threads.
By the time any thread calls getInstance, the instance field is already set, there is no null window to race inside.
No lock, no volatile, no double checking, needed anywhere.

blocks.content: Nothing here is exotic, it is just choosing to do the work earlier instead of later.
The tradeoff

Eager initialization creates the object whether or not it ever gets used. If construction is expensive, for example opening a real database connection, and some code paths never touch the Singleton at all, that work is wasted.
For a cheap object, this tradeoff is almost never worth worrying about, and eager initialization is usually the least risky choice available.
It is also the easiest version to read at a glance, which counts for a lot when someone else has to maintain this code later.
Most real Java codebases end up preferring this holder trick, or the enum version covered next, over the classic double checked lock.
A middle ground worth knowing
Java offers a lazy option that keeps the simplicity of eager initialization, using a private static holder class.

The trick relies on the fact that a nested class is not loaded, and therefore the instance inside it is not created, until something actually references that nested class for the first time. That gives you lazy creation with the same thread safety guarantee as eager initialization, and no explicit locking anywhere.
6. The Enum Based Singleton
Java has one more option that is specific to the language, using an enum with a single value.
The Java language specification guarantees that enum constants are created exactly once, and that creation is inherently thread safe, handled by the JVM itself.
What you get for free

["Thread safety, guaranteed by the JVM, no locks or volatile needed anywhere in your code.","Serialization safety, enums cannot be re-created through deserialization the way a normal class can, so you cannot accidentally end up with a second instance after saving and loading state.","Reflection resistance, the usual trick of calling a private constructor through reflection to create a second instance does not work on enums."]
items: Thread safety, guaranteed by the JVM, no locks or volatile needed anywhere in your code.
Serialization safety, enums cannot be re-created through deserialization the way a normal class can, so you cannot accidentally end up with a second instance after saving and loading state.
Reflection resistance, the usual trick of calling a private constructor through reflection to create a second instance does not work on enums.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499326514-485160214.png
blocks.alt: A single enum Singleton instance providing thread safety, serialization safety, and reflection resistance all from the JVM

blocks.title: Why this feels underused
blocks.content: Many developers do not think of enum as a Singleton tool because it looks like it belongs to a completely different job. Effective Java famously argues this is the best approach available in Java for a simple Singleton, precisely because the language itself closes every loophole that the class based versions have to guard against manually.
When enum is not a fit
blocks.text: When enum is not a fit

blocks.content: An enum based Singleton cannot extend another class, since every enum already implicitly extends Enum. If your Singleton needs to inherit behavior from an existing base class, this approach will not compile.
For the common case of a simple Singleton with no inheritance requirement, this limitation rarely matters in practice.
7. Comparing All The Approaches
With five approaches on the table, a side by side comparison makes the tradeoffs concrete instead of abstract.
Each approach trades away something different. Laying them side by side makes the right default much easier to see.

None of these are wrong in every situation. The right choice depends on how expensive the object is to build, whether the language gives you enum, and how much you value simplicity over squeezing out the last bit of laziness.
Read the table below as a decision aid, not a ranking. The best choice for a tiny logger and the best choice for an expensive database connection manager can be two different rows.

blocks.alt: Double checked locking closing the race, one thread acquires the lock and safely publishes the instance while the other waits and then reads the finished object

8. Which One Should You Actually Reach For
blocks.text: 8. Which One Should You Actually Reach For

blocks.content: If the object is cheap to create, reach for eager initialization first. It is the smallest amount of code, and there is no race condition to reason about because there is no window where the instance is missing.
If you need lazy creation without hand rolling any locking, the static holder class approach gives you that for free in Java, and deserves to be far better known than it is.
If you are in Java specifically and do not need lazy creation, the enum based Singleton is arguably the cleanest option available, since the language closes every backdoor for you.

Reach for double checked locking only when creation is genuinely expensive and you actually need to defer it until first use. Just do not forget volatile, since that single keyword is the difference between a pattern that is famous for working and one that is famous for being broken.
Avoid the plain synchronized method in anything performance sensitive. It is correct, but it pays a lock on every call forever, long after that lock stopped doing any useful work.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499329273-981374568.png
blocks.alt: Decision flow for picking a Singleton approach based on whether the object is cheap to build and whether lazy creation is required

blocks.content: And whichever version you pick, this is one of those rare corners of software where the simplest looking code is the one most likely to be silently wrong. Take the extra minute to reason through what happens when two threads arrive at the same line at the same time.
A quick mental test that helps, imagine two threads pausing at literally the exact same instruction, then ask what each one sees.
If the answer depends on timing you cannot control, the code is not actually thread safe yet, no matter how it reads.
